lessons.title: Week 5 · Day 1 · Relations, functions and uniqueness
lessons.body:
UNIT 2 • FUNCTIONS • DAY 1
Objective: Determine whether each permitted input has exactly one output.
Prerequisites: Unit 1 expressions, equations, inequality boundaries and variable units.

Activate prior knowledge (5 min)
Before solving, define input and output in this situation: Is {(0,2),(1,2),(2,2)} a function? Write one prediction and justify it.

Worked concept and explanation (12 min)
The relation {(1,3),(2,5),(1,7)} is not a function because input 1 has two outputs. {(1,3),(2,5),(3,5)} is a function: repeated outputs are allowed; repeated inputs with different outputs are not.

Learning objective: Determine whether each permitted input has exactly one output. Check each conclusion against the definition or real-world constraint.

Reason together (12 min)
1. Is {(0,2),(1,2),(2,2)} a function? Explain why your conclusion follows from the rule or domain.
2. Is {(−1,4),(−1,9),(3,2)} a function? Explain why your conclusion follows from the rule or domain.

Independent practice (16 min)
1. Classify {(2,8),(3,9),(4,8)}. Show substitutions, domain restrictions or counterexamples as appropriate.
2. Classify {(5,1),(5,1),(6,2)}. Show substitutions, domain restrictions or counterexamples as appropriate.
3. Give a counterexample to the claim that different inputs must have different outputs. Show substitutions, domain restrictions or counterexamples as appropriate.

Individual exit evidence (5 min)
Does {(0,3),(1,4),(0,4)} define a function? Explain. State the conclusion and its supporting reasoning.

Homework and self-assessment (5 min)
Write a new example and nonexample related to today's concept: Determine whether each permitted input has exactly one output. Label inputs and outputs, and include an explanation. Optional challenge: modify the model so its domain changes without changing the algebraic formula.

Accessibility: provide a two-column input/output table, read mathematical symbols aloud, use tactile or enlarged graphs where applicable, permit oral reasoning recorded by the teacher, and provide additional processing time under an approved plan. Extension: justify a counterexample or generalize the rule.
learningTargets: Determine whether each permitted input has exactly one output.
I can communicate function reasoning using a valid input, output, or counterexample.

lessons.title: Week 5 · Day 2 · Evaluate function notation
lessons.body:
UNIT 2 • FUNCTIONS • DAY 2
Objective: Evaluate f(x) and distinguish an input from the output it produces.
Prerequisites: Unit 1 expressions, equations, inequality boundaries and variable units.

Activate prior knowledge (5 min)
Before solving, define input and output in this situation: If g(x)=2x+7, find g(4). Write one prediction and justify it.

Worked concept and explanation (12 min)
For f(x)=3x−4, f(5)=3(5)−4=11, while f(−2)=−6−4=−10. f(5) means the output at input 5, not f multiplied by 5. To find the input with output 11, solve 3x−4=11, obtaining x=5.

Learning objective: Evaluate f(x) and distinguish an input from the output it produces. Check each conclusion against the definition or real-world constraint.

Reason together (12 min)
1. If g(x)=2x+7, find g(4). Explain why your conclusion follows from the rule or domain.
2. If h(x)=x²−1, find h(−3). Explain why your conclusion follows from the rule or domain.

Independent practice (16 min)
1. For f(x)=4x−3, find f(−2). Show substitutions, domain restrictions or counterexamples as appropriate.
2. For p(t)=t²+2t, find p(3). Show substitutions, domain restrictions or counterexamples as appropriate.
3. For q(x)=5−2x, solve q(x)=−1. Show substitutions, domain restrictions or counterexamples as appropriate.

Individual exit evidence (5 min)
If f(x)=2x²−3, find f(−2). State the conclusion and its supporting reasoning.

Homework and self-assessment (5 min)
Write a new example and nonexample related to today's concept: Evaluate f(x) and distinguish an input from the output it produces. Label inputs and outputs, and include an explanation. Optional challenge: modify the model so its domain changes without changing the algebraic formula.

Accessibility: provide a two-column input/output table, read mathematical symbols aloud, use tactile or enlarged graphs where applicable, permit oral reasoning recorded by the teacher, and provide additional processing time under an approved plan. Extension: justify a counterexample or generalize the rule.

lessons.title: Week 5 · Day 3 · Domains from mathematical rules
lessons.body:
UNIT 2 • FUNCTIONS • DAY 3
Objective: Identify input values that make an algebraic rule defined over the real numbers.
Prerequisites: Unit 1 expressions, equations, inequality boundaries and variable units.

Activate prior knowledge (5 min)
Before solving, define input and output in this situation: Find the real domain of 4/(x+1). Write one prediction and justify it.

Worked concept and explanation (12 min)
For f(x)=5/(x−3), x=3 is excluded because division by zero is undefined; the domain is all real x except 3. For g(x)=√(x+2), real outputs require x+2≥0, so x≥−2. For h(x)=x², every real input is allowed.

Learning objective: Identify input values that make an algebraic rule defined over the real numbers. Check each conclusion against the definition or real-world constraint.

Reason together (12 min)
1. Find the real domain of 4/(x+1). Explain why your conclusion follows from the rule or domain.
2. Find the real domain of √(x−5). Explain why your conclusion follows from the rule or domain.

Independent practice (16 min)
1. Find the domain of 7/(2x−6). Show substitutions, domain restrictions or counterexamples as appropriate.
2. Find the domain of √(8−x). Show substitutions, domain restrictions or counterexamples as appropriate.
3. Find the domain of 3x²−2x+1. Show substitutions, domain restrictions or counterexamples as appropriate.

Individual exit evidence (5 min)
Explain why x=−4 cannot be used in f(x)=9/(x+4). State the conclusion and its supporting reasoning.

Homework and self-assessment (5 min)
Write a new example and nonexample related to today's concept: Identify input values that make an algebraic rule defined over the real numbers. Label inputs and outputs, and include an explanation. Optional challenge: modify the model so its domain changes without changing the algebraic formula.

Accessibility: provide a two-column input/output table, read mathematical symbols aloud, use tactile or enlarged graphs where applicable, permit oral reasoning recorded by the teacher, and provide additional processing time under an approved plan. Extension: justify a counterexample or generalize the rule.

lessons.title: Week 5 · Day 4 · Domains from real-world constraints
lessons.body:
UNIT 2 • FUNCTIONS • DAY 4
Objective: Choose a feasible domain using units, whole-number requirements and capacity limits.
Prerequisites: Unit 1 expressions, equations, inequality boundaries and variable units.

Activate prior knowledge (5 min)
Before solving, define input and output in this situation: A ticket booth sells at most 80 whole tickets. State the domain for revenue R(t)=6t. Write one prediction and justify it.

Worked concept and explanation (12 min)
A class pays $12 per student for up to 24 seats. The cost rule C(n)=12n has domain n∈{0,1,2,…,24}; n=2.5 is not a possible student count and n=30 exceeds capacity. Its outputs range from $0 to $288 in increments of $12.

Learning objective: Choose a feasible domain using units, whole-number requirements and capacity limits. Check each conclusion against the definition or real-world constraint.

Reason together (12 min)
1. A ticket booth sells at most 80 whole tickets. State the domain for revenue R(t)=6t. Explain why your conclusion follows from the rule or domain.
2. A tank has 40 liters and drains at 5 liters per minute. Domain for V(t)=40−5t? Explain why your conclusion follows from the rule or domain.

Independent practice (16 min)
1. A team can bring at most 12 players. Domain of P(n)=20n? Show substitutions, domain restrictions or counterexamples as appropriate.
2. A candle burns for 6 hours. Domain of H(t)=15−2.5t? Show substitutions, domain restrictions or counterexamples as appropriate.
3. Explain why a cost function for whole meals should not accept n=3.7. Show substitutions, domain restrictions or counterexamples as appropriate.

Individual exit evidence (5 min)
A theater sells up to 100 tickets at $9 each. State domain and maximum revenue. State the conclusion and its supporting reasoning.

Homework and self-assessment (5 min)
Write a new example and nonexample related to today's concept: Choose a feasible domain using units, whole-number requirements and capacity limits. Label inputs and outputs, and include an explanation. Optional challenge: modify the model so its domain changes without changing the algebraic formula.

Accessibility: provide a two-column input/output table, read mathematical symbols aloud, use tactile or enlarged graphs where applicable, permit oral reasoning recorded by the teacher, and provide additional processing time under an approved plan. Extension: justify a counterexample or generalize the rule.

lessons.title: Week 5 · Day 5 · Function identification and transfer
lessons.body:
UNIT 2 • FUNCTIONS • DAY 5
Objective: Evaluate, classify and constrain functions in a single contextual explanation.
Prerequisites: Unit 1 expressions, equations, inequality boundaries and variable units.

Activate prior knowledge (5 min)
Before solving, define input and output in this situation: For f(x)=2x−5, find f(6) and the input giving output 7. Write one prediction and justify it.

Worked concept and explanation (12 min)
A shuttle charges $6 plus $3 per passenger for up to 14 passengers. C(n)=6+3n with domain n∈{0,…,14}. C(4)=18 dollars. Each input count has exactly one output, so this is a function. The maximum cost is C(14)=$48.

Learning objective: Evaluate, classify and constrain functions in a single contextual explanation. Check each conclusion against the definition or real-world constraint.

Reason together (12 min)
1. For f(x)=2x−5, find f(6) and the input giving output 7. Explain why your conclusion follows from the rule or domain.
2. Does {(1,2),(2,3),(1,3)} define a function? Explain why your conclusion follows from the rule or domain.

Independent practice (16 min)
1. For g(x)=x²−4, find g(−1). Show substitutions, domain restrictions or counterexamples as appropriate.
2. State the domain of h(x)=2/(x−7). Show substitutions, domain restrictions or counterexamples as appropriate.
3. A hall seats 35 people. Revenue R(n)=11n. Give domain and R(12). Show substitutions, domain restrictions or counterexamples as appropriate.

Individual exit evidence (5 min)
Explain why {(2,1),(3,1),(4,1)} is a function and give its range. State the conclusion and its supporting reasoning.

Homework and self-assessment (5 min)
Write a new example and nonexample related to today's concept: Evaluate, classify and constrain functions in a single contextual explanation. Label inputs and outputs, and include an explanation. Optional challenge: modify the model so its domain changes without changing the algebraic formula.

Accessibility: provide a two-column input/output table, read mathematical symbols aloud, use tactile or enlarged graphs where applicable, permit oral reasoning recorded by the teacher, and provide additional processing time under an approved plan. Extension: justify a counterexample or generalize the rule.
